stem: A client frequently misses doses because the medication schedule is complex and easy to forget. Which intervention best supports adherence?

options.A: Keep the current complex dosing schedule unchanged and add extra written instructions, without exploring whether the number of daily dosing times can be reduced.
options.B: Teach the medication purposes and directions, but avoid asking about side effects, cost, confusion, or other factors that may make the regimen difficult to follow.
options.C: Identify the client's barriers, simplify or cluster dosing times when clinically possible, link doses to daily routines, and use a pill organizer or electronic reminder if helpful.
options.D: Ask the client to rely on memory rather than routines or reminder tools so that adherence does not become dependent on external prompts.

rationale: AHRQ Tool 16 recommends asking what makes medication use difficult, considering options that reduce the number of daily doses when clinically appropriate, linking medication-taking to regular daily activities, and using pill organizers or electronic reminders when useful. Therefore C directly addresses both the complex schedule and forgetting. A leaves the complexity unaddressed, B intentionally fails to assess common adherence barriers, and D rejects reminder strategies specifically recommended by AHRQ.
educational_objective: Support medication adherence by identifying individual barriers and making the regimen easier to follow through clinically appropriate schedule simplification, daily routines, and reminder tools.
source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_document_title: Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, 3rd Edition — Help Patients Take Medicine Correctly: Tool 16
source_version_date: Third Edition, 2024; Tool 16 content last reviewed April 2024; live federal source accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: Tool 16 > Actions > Prevent errors > Discuss and resolve patients' concerns / Consider prescribing options; Help patients remember to take their medicines > routines, pill organizers, family support, electronic reminders.
source_claim_supported: Medication-management support includes identifying barriers, reducing dosing frequency or clustering medicines when clinically appropriate, linking doses to daily routines, and using pill organizers or electronic reminders to help patients remember medicines.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — supporting self-management in the home environment

source_original.stem: A client frequently misses doses because the medication schedule is complex and easy to forget. Which intervention best supports adherence?

options.A: Increase the number of daily dosing times when possible because a more complex schedule makes each dose more noticeable and therefore improves adherence.
options.B: Focus on medication education without asking about cost, side effects, or confusion because those barriers are separate from adherence counseling.
options.C: Simplify the regimen when possible, link doses to daily routines, and use pill organizers or electronic reminders tailored to the client's barriers.
options.D: Use counseling without reminder tools because pill organizers, routines, and electronic prompts add complexity without improving day-to-day adherence.

source_original.rationale: Adherence improves when regimens and reminders are made easier and barriers are addressed. Option C is correct because AHRQ recommends simplifying dosing when possible, linking doses to routines, and using pill organizers or electronic reminders. Option A increases complexity. Option B ignores common adherence barriers. Option D rejects practical reminder strategies that AHRQ recommends.
source_original.source_detail: AHRQ Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, Tool 16 — Help Patients Take Medicine Correctly: identify adherence barriers; simplify medication schedules when possible; link doses with daily routines; use pill organizers, charts, family supports, alarms or electronic reminders as appropriate to the individual's barriers. AHRQ Tool 16 last reviewed 2024-04 and remains current on the federal AHRQ site; live source rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Health Promotion and Maintenance: preventive care, immunization, pregnancy health promotion, adherence support and age/risk-appropriate teaching activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the stem, construct and key C. Rewrote the distractors to remove fabricated claims about complexity improving adherence or reminder tools worsening adherence. The final choices now differ by source-supported medication-management actions, and the NCSBN locator was narrowed to home self-management and learning barriers.

audit_findings.source_authority: Federal AHRQ Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, 3rd Edition; NCSBN for blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: Tool 16 last reviewed April 2024 and live-rechecked 2026-08-16; toolkit remains current
audit_findings.exact_locator: AHRQ Tool 16 > Prevent errors and Help patients remember to take their medicines; NCSBN HPM page 9 home-management/learning-barrier activities
audit_findings.claim_audit: Every recommended adherence strategy in C and the rationale appears directly in Tool 16; no invented dose, interval, outcome magnitude, or causal mechanism remains.

distractor_audit.A: Fails to use the AHRQ option of reducing/cluster dosing times and leaves the stated complexity barrier intact.
distractor_audit.B: Conflicts with AHRQ direction to ask about and resolve side-effect, financial, physical, cognitive and logistical barriers.
distractor_audit.C: Directly combines the AHRQ-supported responses to complexity and forgetting.
distractor_audit.D: Conflicts with AHRQ's explicit routine, pill-organizer and electronic-reminder strategies.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C addresses both stated barriers using a fully source-supported strategy set; each other option contains a direct conflict with Tool 16.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are adherence interventions rather than pharmacologic mechanisms; the correct answer is identified by content, not formatting.
audit_findings.blueprint: Health Promotion and Maintenance — client learning barriers and ability to manage care at home.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked AHRQ currentness and exact action sections, all four choices, rationale, objective, NCSBN classification and second-answer risk from zero; C remained uniquely best.
